items.title: Cutting an integral into 100 trapezoids beats analytical integration for most real problems
items.claim: Most integrals appearing in physics, engineering or statistics do NOT have closed-form solutions. They're computed numerically. The simplest method (trapezoidal rule) divides the interval into strips and approximates each as a trapezoid.

options.text: Error in the trapezoidal rule is O(1/n^2) where n is the number of strips. Simpson's rule (quadratic interpolation) is O(1/n^4). Gauss-Legendre and adaptive quadrature can achieve essentially machine precision for well-behaved integrands
Always less accurate than analytical answers

items.reveal:
Trapezoidal rule: approximate integral from a to b of f(x) dx by the sum of trapezoidal strips. Error scales as h^2 (where h is the strip width), so halving h quarters the error.

Simpson's rule (uses quadratic fits to triples of points): error scales as h^4. Halving h reduces error by 16x.

For a function smooth enough on [a, b], Simpson's rule with 20 strips can give 6-7 decimal places of accuracy. Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 10 nodes can give 10-15 decimal places.

Many real-world integrals:
- integral of e^(-x^2) dx: no elementary antiderivative. Used everywhere in statistics. Always computed numerically (or via the error function erf).
- integral of sin(x)/x dx: no elementary form. Defined as the sine integral Si(x).
- integral over irregular domains, multidimensional integrals, integrals with singularities — numerical methods are standard.

Monte Carlo integration: for high-dimensional integrals (d > ~4), grid-based methods (Simpson, Gauss) suffer the 'curse of dimensionality' — n grid points per axis means n^d total. Monte Carlo (random sampling) has error O(1/sqrt(N)) independent of dimension; the standard tool for integrals in 10+ dimensions (e.g., statistical mechanics, finance).

More sophisticated: adaptive quadrature (refines where the function is wiggly), Romberg's method, Chebyshev quadrature for analytic functions, sparse grids, quasi-Monte Carlo with low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol, Halton).

The trade-off between numerical and analytical: analytical is exact when available, but unavailable for most functions. Numerical is universally applicable, with accuracy dialed up by computational cost.
items.why: Calculus class focuses on analytical integration. Real applied math is largely numerical — and the numerical methods can be vastly faster and more accurate than the analytical ones for the integrals actually needed.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.

items.title: In London, there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs
items.claim: Humans have at most about 150,000 hairs on their heads. London has over 9 million people. By the pigeonhole principle, at least 60 Londoners share an EXACT hair count.

options.text: If you put more than n items into n containers, at least one container has at least 2 items; more generally, if k*n + 1 items go into n containers, some container has at least k + 1

items.reveal:
The pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's drawer principle, 1834): if you put n + 1 objects into n boxes, at least one box has at least 2 objects.

Applied to London: ~9 million heads, at most ~150,000 possible hair counts. 9 million divided by 150,000 = 60. So at least 60 Londoners share a hair count exactly.

Elegant applications:
- In any group of 367 people, two share a birthday (366 possible birthdays + leap year).
- Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three mutual strangers (a Ramsey theory result, R(3,3) = 6).
- Among any 10 distinct integers from 1 to 100, two have a sum or difference divisible by 17.
- In any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős-Szekeres).

The principle gives existence proofs without constructing the example. It's surprisingly powerful for such a simple idea.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle looks obvious but yields non-trivial results — existence guarantees from pure counting, often where direct construction is hopeless.
